items.title: The 10 Greatest Video Game Masterpieces of the Last 5 Years, Ranked
items.summary: Donkey Kong Bonanza, Alan Wake II and Baldur's Gate 3 are among the best video games of the last five years that can truly be considered masterpieces.
items.content:
clair-obscur-expedition-33-characters.jpg Image via Sandfall Entertainment By Lucas Kloberdanz-Dyck Published Sep 30, 2026, 8:20 AM EDT Lucas Kloberdanz-Dyck is a writer for Collider. He grew up creating lists, stories, and worlds, which led to his love of anime and video games. He attended Sheridan College where he earned an Honours Bachelor of Game Design. Lucas and his group won 1st place for technical innovation at LevelUp Toronto 2023, and he was also an intern for the Oakville Film Festival of Arts. Sign in to your Collider account Add Us Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Video games continue to evolve more and more with each passing year, growing from classic titles such as The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time to modern sensations like Red Dead Redemption 2 . While it is fascinating to see where gaming will go next, the past five years in particular have been home to some of the best games of all time.

It is strange to think that it has already been five years since 2021, because in that time some of the best games came out. That is why this list will celebrate ten video game masterpieces from the last five years based on aspects such as gameplay, design, narrative, visuals, originality, entertainment value, fan opinion, critical acclaim, and overall quality.

Kratos and Atreus standing together in God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment A still from God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment A still from God of War: Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment Kratos holding Mimir in God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment Thor staring down menacingly at Heimdall in God of War: Ragnarok Image via PlayStation Studios Close Kratos and Atreus standing together in God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment A still from God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment A still from God of War: Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment Kratos holding Mimir in God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment Thor staring down menacingly at Heimdall in God of War: Ragnarok Image via PlayStation Studios window.arrayOfGalleries["article-gallery-1-889878468"] = '" Kratos and Atreus standing together in God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment A still from God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment A still from God of War: Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment Kratos holding Mimir in God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment Thor staring down menacingly at Heimdall in God of War: Ragnarok Image via PlayStation Studios Close Kratos and Atreus standing together in God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment A still from God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment A still from God of War: Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment Kratos holding Mimir in God of War Ragnarok Image via Sony Interactive Entertainment Thor staring down menacingly at Heimdall in God of War: Ragnarok Image via PlayStation Studios "'; This list has a surprising amount of sequels, including some that were up for Game of the Year, such as God of War Ragnarök . Set shortly after the first game, Fimbulwinter is here, meaning the titular apocalypse event is soon approaching. However, Kratos and Atreus launch a siege on the gods, hoping this will save the realm from destruction.

God of War Ragnarök isn’t better than its predecessor, but it is still a masterpiece from the past five years. The plot does a great job of depicting the spectacle of the event while also focusing on the grounded and emotional parts of the core narrative , specifically regarding the relationship between Kratos and Atreus. God of War Ragnarök is a heartfelt and epic gaming classic.

An 8-bit mouse using a spiked ball on the end of a whip while on a bridge in 'Mina the Hollower' Image via Yacht Club Games 2026 isn’t over yet, but it is already full of remarkable titles, and one of the frontrunners for best game is Mina the Hollower . The titular character ventures to the land of Tenebrous to fix its generator. However, players uncover an even greater darkness and must fight the unrestricted progress of humanity and technology.

Mina the Hollower is already one of the best video games of 2026 , and it does this as an indie title. The retro aesthetic and worldbuilding contribute to a visually stunning setting, but what’s more is its unique mechanics that make the gameplay fluid and kinetic . Mina the Hollower is an underrated gem and a magnificent indie effort that proves the genre is at its peak in the last five years.

A group of characters on a field in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Image via Sandfall Entertainment While 2026 isn’t over yet, 2025 came and went with some incredible games in stock, including what is undoubtedly considered the best, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . An entity known as the paintress erases an age from the planet every year, and the world's efforts have so far been useless. But with the 33rd try, they hope to stop this villain and save the rest of the world.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was the unanimous Game of the Year winner in 2025 , and it earned this honor because of its blend of compelling narrative, intense combat, and unique art style . Besides being visually gorgeous, this game is also innovative with its mix of turn-based combat and real-time events that create an immersive and engaging style of gameplay.

A hand of playing cards being used in a round of 'Balatro' Image via LocalThunk Mina the Hollower may have been the first indie game on here, but it won’t be the last, because following it is Balatro . This poker-themed roguelike has players building decks to defeat the hands of the enemy, and with each match the difficulty increases, as does the entertainment.

Balatro is quick to play and easy to understand, but its true genius lies in the ability to break the game since it allows players to create any sort of hand they want. This addictive video game is fast-paced but demanding , forcing the player's attention at all times and keeping them engaged with the gameplay and sensory feedback that is a visual explosion. All these elements prove why it's a video game that is a blast .

A young Pauline in shock in Donkey Kong Bananza Image via Nintendo Nintendo has had a magnificent five years, from all-time sales numbers to the Nintendo Switch 2. One game on the latter that wowed everyone was Donkey Kong Bananza . As Void Company tries to steal all the bananas in the world for their selfish wish, DK and Pauline travel through the core of the world to stop them, and maybe get their own wish as well.

Fans desperately want a new 3D Mario, but Donkey Kong Bananza is such a novel idea that it not only acted as a suitable alternative, but it also became one of Nintendo's most imaginative games . The smashing gameplay never gets old, and the new world keeps the gameplay fresh. Donkey Kong Bananza is a one-of-a-kind game that shows why Nintendo is known for its creativity.

Preview of Alan Wake and Saga in Alan Wake 2 video game Image via Remedy Entertainment 2023 was one of the best years for video games in a long time, and one of the three best games from this year is Alan Wake II . Gamers play as the titular novelist who is trying to escape an alternate dimension. But at the same time, a detective is investigating a murder that is suspiciously similar to one of Alan Wake’s murder mystery novels.

Alan Wake II is absolutely beautiful, but not in a traditional way; rather, it uses its inherent weirdness and mind-bending aspects alongside real cutscenes to deliver a surreal gaming experience . This unique and unforgettable title is mysterious and suspenseful, offering a compelling narrative enhanced by a distinct visual identity, which ended up making it one of the most beloved video games of the 2020s .

items.title: 5 Near-Perfect RPGs You Should Play in 2026
items.summary: The best modern RPGs are must-play games, and if you haven't played titles like Clair Obscur in 2026, you're missing out.
items.content:
clair obscur expedition 33 featured art Image via Sandfall Interactive By Shawn Wilken Published Sep 28, 2026, 12:30 PM EDT Shawn Wilken is an avid anime and manga fan for most of his life, and is best known for his work in journalism spanning that time, working as a credentialed sports writer for LastWordOnSports.com, before transitioning to a gaming and anime writer. Joining CBR, Shawn brings a wealth of knowledge in the anime and manga industry and over two decades of journalism experience. Sign in to your CBR account Add Us Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread 2 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap RPGs are one of the most popular gaming genres, and while many games include some role-playing elements, there's nothing quite like the experience of playing a full-fledged RPG. Classic RPGs like Fallout and Diablo II continue to be favorites, but there have also been several amazing RPGs released in the last few years that fans of the genre won't want to miss out on.

The RPG genre is alive and well in 2026, and while there are new games like Crimson Desert to enjoy, it's worth catching up on the best RPGs of the last few years before diving into new titles. These games all received rave reviews when they launched, and somehow, they go beyond expectations.

Close Image via Larian Image via Larian Studios Astarion smiling in Baldur's Gate 3 Image via Larian Studios window.arrayOfGalleries["article-gallery-1-1660005009"] = '" Close Image via Larian Image via Larian Studios Astarion smiling in Baldur's Gate 3 Image via Larian Studios "'; Baldur's Gate 3 offers a degree of choice and consequence rarely seen in RPGs. Players are dropped into the Forgotten Realms while infected with a mind-flayer parasite, embarking on a thrilling quest that shifts between complex political intrigue and intense turn-based battles. The graphics use a detailed cinematic engine that renders expressive facial animations and intricate spell effects beautifully.

The core gameplay relies on an adaptation of the Dungeons & Dragons Fifth Edition rulebook , granting gamers freedom to customize classes and exploit physics. The digital sandbox is completely open for action, as a single scenario can be resolved through witty dialogue or by casting a fireball on a flammable puddle.

The difficulty level in Baldur's Gate 3 is notoriously flexible, offering everything from a story-focused option to a brutal Honor Mode that grants enemies legendary actions and deletes save files upon a total party wipe. Because the game engine supports endless variable paths for every quest line, a global community remains heavily engaged in discovering hidden variables and fresh tactical approaches.

Image via FromSoftware The Lands Between represent a masterclass in open-world design, trading quest markers and map clutter for pure, uninterrupted exploration. The visuals are legendary for their breathtaking art direction, with underworld vistas that look like dark fantasy oil paintings come to life. Players step into the shoes of a Tarnished warrior guided only by faint trails of grace,

Elden Ring 's combat mechanics require immense concentration and precision. Despite its difficulty, Elden Ring offers a tremendous sense of freedom, as the game lets players ride past overwhelming threats or tackle regional dungeons in a completely non-linear order to gather strength.

With the monumental addition of the Shadow of the Erdtree expansion, the active player base remains incredibly robust. Elden Ring rewards meticulous attribute allocation and experimental gear synergy, offering over a hundred distinct weapon types ranging from swift light greatswords to volatile sorceries. The lack of artificial hand-holding makes it a rewarding triumph.

Close Keanu Reeves in Cyberpunk 2077 Image via CD Projekt Red Official art for Cyberpunk 2077 v getting into a gun fight with police Image via CD PROJEKT RED Image of maelstrom being hostile towards player in Cyberpunk 2077 Image via user Eris404 window.arrayOfGalleries["article-gallery-2-401317309"] = '" Close Keanu Reeves in Cyberpunk 2077 Image via CD Projekt Red Official art for Cyberpunk 2077 v getting into a gun fight with police Image via CD PROJEKT RED Image of maelstrom being hostile towards player in Cyberpunk 2077 Image via user Eris404 "'; Cyberpunk 2077 introduces V, a mercenary fighting for survival against a ticking digital consciousness, through a dark future dominated by corporate espionage and street warfare. Night City is a neon-soaked metropolis divided into six visually and culturally distinct districts, and the result is one of the best cities in open-world history.

The heavily overhauled gameplay framework allows for complete freedom of approach , enabling players to specialize in high-speed gunplay or stealthy, long-range cybernetic hacking. This level of cyberware integration provides immense satisfaction, letting players alter V's body to unlock midair dashes and bullet deflection.

2015 to 2025 produced some of the best RPGs ever made, with games that rival or exceed the greatest titles in the history of the genre.

Cyberpunk 2077 continues to maintain a highly active, dedicated following thanks to the massive mechanical evolution brought about by the 2.0 update and the Phantom Liberty expansion. The intricate first-person perspective ensures absolute immersion, and character progression feels deeply rewarding from start to finish.

monster-hunter-wilds-seikret-mount pose Monster Hunter Wilds delivers breathtaking environmental fidelity , showcasing massive sandstorms, sudden electrical downpours and thriving seasons of abundance that sweep across the terrain in real time. The open-world framework connects wilderness regions without a single loading screen, allowing for chaotic turf wars to unfold organically across the landscape.

The core role-playing mechanics center around a satisfying, weapon-based framework utilizing 14 distinct armaments that feature incredibly fluid, expanded movesets. The addition of the Seikret mount lets players manage their inventory on the move and swap between primary weapon types on the fly to exploit localized soft spots on a target.

items.title: Why isn't GTA 6 in the Golden Joystick Awards?
items.content:
GTA 6 isn't eligible for this year's Golden Joystick Awards

(Image credit: Rockstar) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 25 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter GTA 6 will not be eligible to match the records set by Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and Baldur's Gate 3 by completing a sweep of all five major GOTY awards in the 2026/7 season.

The 44th Golden Joystick Awards were announced earlier today , confirming that this year's show will take place on November 11 – eight days before the GTA 6 release date of November 19. Public voting will begin on September 25 for most categories, ending on October 23, before voting for Ultimate Game of the Year runs from October 26-30. That's several weeks before the general public will get its hands on Rockstar's latest, which means it's not eligible for any of this year's awards.

Depending on exactly how you look at it, that means GTA 6 won't be eligible for a full awards sweep. Typically, the 'big five' GOTY awards season begins with the Golden Joysticks in November and ends with the BAFTAs in April, factoring in the Game Awards in December, February's DICE Awards, and March's GDC Awards. But with GTA not releasing until after the 2026 Golden Joystick ceremony, the sweep is out of its grasp.

GTA 6 will be eligible for the 2027 Joysticks, and should it win the biggest prize at The Game Awards you could argue it had still made a delayed sweep. But the record set by Baldur's Gate 3 and matched by Clair Obscur relied on winning the big five across a single awards season, and there's really no way that GTA would be able to do that.

If I were a betting man, I'd suggest that GTA 6 is likely to win all of those awards, even if it has to wait until November 2027. Assuming that comes to pass, you might argue that the sweep still stands, it was just a little late. Purists, however, might disagree, arguing that the only way to get a sweep is to win all five prizes in one go. One thing is for sure though - by the time the BAFTAs roll around next spring, Larian and Sandfall will remain the only studios to complete the sweep.

items.title: Clair Obscur Expedition 33 Director Comments on Sandfall's Next Game
items.summary: Sandfall Interactive doesn't seem too worried about living up to GOTY expectations
items.content:
By Polygon Staff & Willa Rowe Published Sep 14, 2026, 1:06 AM EDT FYI Sandfall Interactive doesn't seem too worried about living up to GOTY expectations

Image: Sandfall Interactive/Kepler Interactive Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , the debut game from developer Sandfall Interactive, was a smash hit in 2025 and earned numerous game of the year awards . The studio's next project, whatever it may be, might not be as popular. Director Guillaume Broche knows Clair Obscur is a tough act to follow, and he's OK if no one likes what the studio does next.

In a lengthy episode of Video Game Club on the Konbini YouTube channel in July, Broche discusses Sandfall's next game and says, "Maybe people won't like it. That's life." It is a surprisingly laid-back attitude toward following up one of the most beloved games in recent memory. For Broche, it isn't any different from the ethos he and the rest of the team at Sandall Interactive had while making Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . "We didn't make the first game to please anyone," he confesses, "and I think that's why it worked." Rather than pleasing an imaginary audience, Broche reveals that development on Clair Obscur was focused on satisfying the developers. They made a game that excited them. It was just an added bonus that plenty of players enjoyed the game as well.

The process obviously worked, and Broche sees no reason to mess with it, despite mounting expectations brought on by the success of Clair Obscur . He admits that there is definitely pressure to make things bigger or to expand the studio because of the attention Sandfall Interactive now has for its next project. Ultimately, Broche says that this would only result in the studio making games that he doesn't actually want to play.

As for Sandfall's next project, Broche declined to share details but did reveal the team will make some drastic decisions. A big question is whether the studio's next game will be a sequel to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . In the interview, Broche reiterates the idea he's shared before that "Clair Obscur" is the name of the franchise and Expedition 33 is just one story the team wanted to tell. This could mean Sandfall will take an anthology approach like in Final Fantasy , with each entry introducing a new world and cast of characters. Returning to the world of Expedition 33 in a true sequel would also require Sandfall to choose a canon ending for the game, something the studio has deliberately avoided. In any case, whatever follows Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 will be worth watching.

items.title: 5 Best Video Games Like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: If you enjoyed Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and are looking for more games that have a similar feel or play style, here are five that should tickle your fancy.
items.content:
Sandfall Interactive Add SVG on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover One of the best video games of 2025 was "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33," developed by French studio Sandfall Interactive. Among the best RPGs outside of "Final Fantasy," the game relies on turn-based combat as it weaves an engrossing epic tale with memorable characters. The story is set in a fantasy vision of France's Belle Époque as a group of adventurers set out to save their community from a mysterious villain known as the artist. With a dazzlingly original world brought to life by sharp writing and engaging gameplay, "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" reminds gamers what's possible with turn-based RPGs.

Of course, "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" has worn its influences on its sleeve and there are plenty of similar turn-based RPGs worth giving a try. From the games that inspired the 2025 title to releases that have gameplay systems that resemble "Clair Obscur," we've rounded up our favorites. Many of these games are cornerstones in the industry when it comes to stellar turn-based RPGs. These are the five best video games like "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" that fans should check out next.

Nintendo Nintendo and Square formed a tight partnership during the Super Nintendo era, with acclaimed titles like "Chrono Trigger" and "Secret of Mana" coming to the console. One game during this period that feels notably similar to "Clair Obscur" is "Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars," originally released in 1996. The game has Mario join a new team of friends, including Geno and Mallow, as they battle the villainous Smithy Gang that's invading the Mushroom Kingdom. Combat unfolds from a turn-based system, but real-time elements are included to make techniques more effective when input properly.

While "Super Mario RPG" is the most playful game on this list in regard to its tonal qualities, its gameplay mechanics definitely serve as a precursor for "Clair Obscur." But the game is a bold reinvention of what a "Super Mario" title can be, further proving that Nintendo's flagship character was more than a platforming protagonist. Nintendo released a remake of "Super Mario RPG," reimagining the classic for the Switch in 2023, wisely staying faithful to the SNES source material. While the Nintendo game and "Clair Obscur" may not share that much at first glance, that combat system and its surprisingly deep world connects the two titles.

Sony Interactive Entertainment Nearly 30 years after its initial release, "The Legend of Dragoon" is among the forgotten PS1 exclusives. A medieval fantasy RPG for a console with a game library full of them, the 1999 title follows the protagonist Dart searching for the figure who murdered his parents. Dart is joined by several playable allies in the campaign who gain the ability to temporarily transform into magical beings through what's referred to as a Dragoon Spirit. The game's combat system is its most unique aspect, revolving around turn-based inputs but in a quick time event sequence to string together combos.

It's this combat system and the general aesthetics around "The Legend of Dragoon" that reminds us of "Clair Obscur" when we play it. This is augmented by the game's transformation mechanic, allowing access to different and more powerful techniques for each character. Through a prominent use of its richly rendered in-game cinematics, the game also places a strong emphasis on its narrative, adding to the stakes. While overshadowed by titles like "Final Fantasy" and "Chrono Cross" on the PS1, "The Legend of Dragoon" definitely deserves more recognition.

Square Enix Of all the "Final Fantasy" games that align with "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33," the closest the fan-favorite franchise gets is "Final Fantasy X." A title from 2001 that changed gaming forever , the story has an athlete named Tidus who is transported to the world of Spira. Teaming up with a group of adventurers, including the powerful summoner Yuna, Tidus sets out to stop the villainous Sin from destroying the world. The game's combat system returns to more traditional turn-based gameplay rather than the Active Time Battle mechanics in prior entries, which included real-time elements.

Just looking at the broader narrative, "Final Fantasy X" and "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" both have a similar setup and stakes, albeit executed in very different ways. But the extensive party system in "Final Fantasy X" also evokes "Clair Obscur," allowing players to freely swap out members in combat. "Final Fantasy" has since largely moved away from turn-based combat, but "Final Fantasy X" still maintains its fun factor 25 years later. One of the best "Final Fantasy" games of all time , "Final Fantasy X" redefined the franchise for the 21st century.

Sega The "Persona" RPG series has been a staple for 30 years and feels bigger than ever, especially in regard to international audiences instead of only its native Japan. The best in the franchise to date is "Persona 5," originally released in 2016 for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation 4. Since then, the game received an enhanced remaster, rebranded as "Persona 5 Royal" in 2019 while significantly expanding its availability on other platforms. The game's story has its protagonist, Joker, transfer to a new high school and tap into his powers to take on shadowy supernatural threats.

"Persona 5" is an ambitious blend of RPG combat, dungeon-crawling exploration, and social simulator elements within the context of its high school setting. Somehow, all of these disparate elements come together beautifully, with its dungeon-crawling planning complementing its combat system especially well. Like "Clair Obscur," the game also has a striking menu layout that keeps players engaged with the action, never overstaying its welcome. Perfectly accessible if you've never played another game in the series, "Persona 5" is a modern RPG masterpiece.

Sega While the "Yakuza" series was initially built around real-time third-person beat'em-up gameplay, the franchise pivoted in a big way with "Yakuza: Like a Dragon." The 2020 game introduces new protagonist Ichiban Kasuga but also pivots to turn-based combat instead of the series' typical real-time brawling. The game also shifts its setting to Yokohama as Kasuga tries to make a name for himself in the world of organized crime in Japan. Kasuga can recruit parties of up to four characters to participate in these battles, mixing hard-hitting action with the series' penchant for wacky humor.

The shift to turn-based gameplay that "Yakuza: Like a Dragon" took could've turned out disastrously in lesser hands, but the game gives the whole series a fresh energy that elevates it as it solidifies its place in the current console generation. The game also incorporates quick time mechanics that help enhance the combat, keeping players engaged both defensively and offensively, like "Clair Obscur" and its own combat timing. "Yakuza: Like a Dragon" provides a boldly new direction for the long-running series.

items.title: Shuhei Yoshida told Expedition 33 studio to avoid terms like 'turn-based RPG' because it may cause people to "overlook" the game
items.summary: The perceived negative stigma around the term 'turn-based RPG' has led Shuhei Yoshida to advise Expedition 33 developers to avoid using it.
items.content:
Image credit: Sandfall / Eurogamer News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Aug. 18, 2026, 8:29 a.m. 37 comments Follow Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Prioritise us on Google One of the reasons Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 stood out so much in early footage was how action-packed its combat looked, despite being a turn-based RPG. But while developer Sandfall Interactive has described the game as a turn-based RPG - and reinvigorated the genre, to some degree - not everyone was happy with that approach.

Veteran PlayStation executive Shuhei Yoshida revealed at the Busan Indie Connect Festival 2026 over the weekend that he warned Expedition 33 developers not to give the game that label (via Automaton ).

Yoshida was impressed by the game's combat, likening it to The Legend of Dragoon's, a game he was the producer of. However, his advice was for the team to pick a different term to describe the game, since he believed 'turn-based RPG' is an outdated term to some players, who could end up dismissing the game as a result.

"It's incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG. That alone might cause players to overlook it," Yoshida said, as reported by 4Gamer .

Yoshida, who worked as an advisor to publishers and developers around the time of his departure from PlayStation in 2025 , revealed the anecdote in a panel aimed at helping indie developers pick the right publisher for their games and making a convincing pitch. As part of his consulting work, he worked with Expedition 33 publisher Kepler Interactive, where he got to play a demo of the game two years before its launch.

According to the report, Kepler and Sandfall took his advice, using the more modern 'reactive turn-based battles' term to describe the game's combat instead. As anyone who played the game will attest, Expedition 33's brand of turn-based combat, which melds real-time mechanics like parrying and dodging with traditional turn orders, became one of the strongest and most-lauded aspects of the game .

Regardless of how much you think Yoshida's advice helped, the success of the game is hard to deny. Expedition 33 initially managed to sell a fitting 3.3 million copies in its first month , before bumping that to 5.5 million copies by October 2025.

It's also been one of the highest-rated games of 2025, winning multiple honours at The Game Awards that year, and ending up at number two on Eurogamer's list of the 50 best games of 2025 .

items.title: Former PlayStation boss Shuhei Yoshida told Clair Obscur devs to not call it a 'turn-based RPG' so people wouldn't 'overlook' it
items.summary: More than eight million copies sold suggests he might
items.content:
More than eight million copies sold suggests he might've been right.

(Image credit: Sandfall Interactive / Kepler Interactive) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 14 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter According to former PlayStation boss Shuhei Yoshida, turn-based RPGs, particularly JRPGs, were so unpopular several years ago that he would tell indie developers to avoid using the term altogether in their marketing—even for a game like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.

Yoshida recalled giving the Clair Obscur developers this advice during a lecture at the Busan Indie Connect Festival 2026 (via Automaton ). He was impressed by a demo he played a couple of years before the game was out, particularly its similarities to The Legend of Dragoon, a game he produced, but recommended the developers at Sandfall Interactive find alternative ways to describe its combat.

"It's incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG," he said. "That alone might cause players to overlook it."

Sandfall listened and started describing Clair Obscur's combat as "reactive turn-based battles" in its marketing. It's hard to tell if that actually had an impact on the breakout success of the game, but it probably didn't hurt.

Even if you set aside the supposed genre stigma, I think calling Clair Obscur a turn-based RPG does undercut how active the combat actually feels. It isn't the kind of game where you can get up and grab a snack in between turns. You're encouraged to study how enemies move so you can time all your dodges and parries, as if you're playing a soulslike.

Clair Obscur is flawed on purpose, says director: 'Games that try to be perfect, that try to fix all their flaws—they're usually just really boring' Even though turn-based and real time RPGs 'have their loud, vocal advocates,' Fallout developer Tim Cain thinks they both have a place in the genre 'If you're designing an RPG, you have to go back to the source:' The post-apocalyptic RPG Entropy takes notes from Fallout and a long-abandoned Warhammer spinoff Did adding a single word before "turn-based" change everything? I'm not convinced it was the sole reason the game caught people's attention when it already looked fast-paced in trailers. But it does speak to the tendency for many games in the genre to only appeal to people who grew up with them, and the number of people who fall asleep when threatened with having to take turns during the action.

Thankfully, Clair Obscur has helped make turn-based games cool again. It sold 3.3 million copies in the first month and has since surpassed eight million copies as of April. Yoshida believes Clair Obscur is a great example of why chasing industry trends isn't always the right move. He also said that publishers have started to see a slew of turn-based games pitched to them in the wake of Clair Obscur's explosive success.

items.title: 'It's Incredibly Well-Made, But…' — Former PlayStation Boss Warned Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Devs It Would Be 'Overlooked' if They Called It a Turn-Based RPG
items.summary: Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it.
items.content:
Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it."

Yoshida, who served as PlayStation's head of indies and president of Sony Interactive Entertainment Worldwide Studios before stepping down in 2024, spoke about some key advice he gave the award-winning team during a recent lecture for indie game developers. Portions of that lecture were then reported by 4Gamer and subsequently translated by Automaton , including one piece of advice he gave to publisher Kepler Interactive while advising the team ahead of its April 2025 launch.

"It’s incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG," Yoshida warned the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 devs. "That alone might cause players to overlook it."

But why? Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 went on to receive praise from fans and critics (including a 9/10 review from IGN), while ending its already explosive year with big wins across The Game Awards , BAFTA , DICE , and IGN award shows. Its positive reception was so intense that even the developers at Sandfall Interactive weren't prepared for its towering Metacritic score .

Yoshida acknowledged Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 as a quality release long before it reached the hands of the public. He was impressed early on, calling attention to its "combination of turn-based JRPG mechanics and real-time action inputs reminiscent of The Legend of Dragoon." The problem, however, was that, at the time, he was concerned its success could be affected by what he observed to be a tendency for turn-based JRPGs to be seen as outdated.

Game-award-winning formula or not, Yoshida feared Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 would be ignored by some gamers if they saw that "turn-based" label. As a result, Kepler got creative and instead started selling Sandfall's first game as an experience with "reactive turn-based battles" instead, and the rest is history.

The game, of course, went on to become a massive sales success despite its proximity to the launch of The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion . Yoshida said he's since noticed an uptick in reports from publishers receiving pitches for new turn-based RPGs.

While we wait to see what's next from Yoshida and Sandfall, you can see why the developers behind Final Fantasy Resonance think turn-based RPGs are making a huge comeback . You can also read the devs' conversation about canon endings and the writer who got their start at Sandfall .

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 director says eliminating limitations in development is a "big mistake." We talk to Sandfall Interactive about staying small, Japanese influences, and what's next
items.summary: Interview with Sandfall Interactive at the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem in Yokohama, Japan.
items.content:
Home Interviews Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 director says eliminating limitations in development is a “big mistake.” We talk to Sandfall Interactive about staying small, Japanese influences, and what’s next Interview with Sandfall Interactive at the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem in Yokohama, Japan.

Game Development , Interviews 2026-07-29 00:00 Genki 3 Epic Games Japan and Sandfall Interactive recently hosted a Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem event in Yokohama, Japan, offering a behind-the-scenes look at the development of 2025’s Game of the Year. After the presentation, AUTOMATON sat down with the developers to discuss their Japanese influences, their views on JRPGs, why Unreal Engine was the right choice for their small team, and why the studio has no intention of significantly increasing its headcount.

Participants are as follows: Guillaume Broche – Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director Tom Guillermin – Sandfall Interactive Co-founder and CTO Alan Reynaud – Lead Character and Concept Artist Alexandre Breton – Technical Artist

For more about Sandfall Interactive’s views on physical disc production ending , check out part two of this interview.

—Could you tell me about the influence Japanese games and anime have had on your approach to game design? What were some of the biggest Japanese influences on Expedition 33?

Guillaume Broche: Growing up, I’d say 95% of the games I was playing were Japanese games, so I’ve always been super influenced by them. My first real video game memory was Final Fantasy VIII on PS1. Before that, I’d also played some games on the Mega Drive, but they were smaller titles and I don’t remember them very well because I was too young. But to this day, JRPGs in particular continue to be one of my favorite genres.

And of course, one of the main influences in my life is the Final Fantasy series and the work of Hironobu Sakaguchi, including titles like Lost Odyssey and Blue Dragon. Other JRPGs that have influenced me include the Shin Megami Tensei and Persona series, the Atelier series, and Tales of Vesperia. I’ve said it a million times by now, but I pretty much play almost all JRPGs available at the time. Not every single one, but really a lot.

Obviously, Expedition 33’s gameplay is very much inspired by the older Final Fantasy games. It’s turn-based, and you have three characters facing three monsters, so they were definitely a massive inspiration.

Also, as I grew up, I think I’d been missing that kind of game ever since Lost Odyssey. Lost Odyssey was, for me, the last big realistic turn-based game. You still have titles like Yakuza and Persona coming out now, but they’re more stylized. On the other hand, I felt like the grand, epic, realistic kind of turn-based games like Final Fantasy X and Last Odyssey didn’t exist anymore. Since that’s my favorite type of game personally, I just wanted to make it.

—How about anime? I believe you’ve mentioned being a big Ghibli fan, but have you drawn influence from any specific titles?

Guillaume Broche: Yes, I know that for a lot of people in the West, Disney is a big part of their childhood memories, but for me, it’s Ghibli. Especially Spirited Away. I think I’ve seen that movie 50 times, no joke. It’s a masterpiece from A to Z, and I also love other films by the studio.

Also, I think one of the anime that inspired me for Expedition 33’s story was Attack on Titan. I really like the idea of a group of heroes fighting together, and I especially love the uniform. When you see any character from Attack on Titan, you instantly know they’re an Attack on Titan character because of the uniform. That’s something I really wanted to bring over into Expedition 33, making the game recognizable just from its uniforms.

In fact, I’m rewatching Attack on Titan right now because I haven’t watched it for at least six years. I’m on season four now, almost at the end, and really, it’s an absolute masterpiece for me.

Alan Reynaud: For the characters, there were a lot of anime that had a big influence on us. One of them is Bleach. I have to mention Bleach because the character designs in the series are spectacular. One of the things we took from it was designs that are super simple yet incredibly memorable. We wanted to have something like that, with a “rule of cool” approach. I’d say that was a big inspiration for the character creation.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 & the Beauty of a Non-Definitive Ending
items.summary: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 gives Maelle and Verso two painful endings. This feature examines grief, escapism, and why neither choice is wrong.
items.content:
Imagine: it’s PAX West 2025, and you’re me, wandering the expo hall with hundreds if not thousands of others. It’s a sea of people, but amongst them, you start to notice an incredibly peculiar pattern: dotting the crowd are bright red French berets. You cross direct paths with someone and notice their red beret is not only accompanied by a black-and-white striped shirt, but a red checked sash, strapping a fake plastic baguette to their back. You’re immediately both intrigued and perplexed, and raise the obvious question to your partner, who explains it’s from that game he started playing “with Charlie Cox in it”.

In this scenario, you are very much a fan of Charlie Cox and his starring in Daredevil, so you’re immediately reminded of what he’s talking about in that explanation – Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. You vaguely remember seeing the first casting announcement trailer for it during a random State of Play one early morning and getting excited because Daredevil(!), but ultimately you ended up going back to your endless, hellish cycle of Marvel Rivals lobbies when the game actually released. The red berets are a kind reminder of your previous excitement about the game, though, and it isn’t long after that you find yourself glued to your television while being serenaded by a beautiful French accent as you are formally introduced to the citizens of Lumiere. Your four years of French classes throughout school surely prepared you for this moment.

What you aren’t prepared for is just how much of an effect this game has on you by the end.

Now, at the risk of being honest, it’s a complete understatement to say I love this game. If you have interacted with me within the last year, I have talked to you about this game, or I have told you to finish it after you told me you didn’t even get through Act I, or I have endlessly gushed over Lorien Testard’s soundtrack what was probably an annoying amount. It’s rare to find yourself so committed to a piece of media, if only because you see yourself reflected in it so wholly, whether it’s in Maelle’s escapism or Verso’s self-sacrificial tendencies. After all, you don’t win 37 awards because people just feel pretty okay emotions about your game. As is with any piece of media, though, comes what others have to say about it.

(Obligatory note: What’s discussed going forward is riding off of the notion that the person reading this has played the game. If you haven’t, maybe go open Steam or the PlayStation store, grab some tissues, strap in for a bit, and hopefully you will thank me later. Or feel free to keep reading – I’m certainly not stopping you).

One of the gaming community’s most divisive conversations regarding Expedition 33 is regarding the two distinct endings the game has to offer, notwithstanding how both are unique in how they highlight the game’s central theme around the idea of grief. There hasn’t been a day that’s gone by in recent memory where I haven’t been faced with someone explaining how “[insert your preferred character’s name] ending is the right one”, or “if you chose [insert your not-preferred character’s name] ending, you’re clearly heartless”.

In the first ending, the audience is brought back to Lumiere after Maelle and Verso’s battle, and we see that Maelle has not erased the canvas, which was her motivation by the end of Act III. We’re rejoined by the ensemble we’ve grown to love, the Expeditioners as well as Esquie and Monoco, and we even see that Gustave and Sophie have both been repainted after their previous deaths. We’re also faced with Maelle and a considerably older Verso. We see Verso struggle for an uncomfortable moment, his hands stretching out and freezing over keys of a grand piano in Lumiere’s opera house, until it can be discerned Maelle uses her Paintress abilities in order to force the painted version of her late brother to play.

The colors are washed. The lighting is dimmed. It doesn’t yield much comfort aside from the embrace of familiar faces, but that just might be enough.

The second ending is an intentionally stark contrast. For the first time in the game, we’re officially brought outside of the canvas now that it’s presumably been destroyed, as that was Verso’s desire by the end game, and we’re shown the Dessendre’s. In front of them sits a grave donning the name “Verso Dessendre”. Renoir and Aline share a tender embrace in front of their son’s grave, Clea leaves behind a bouquet of achingly familiar red and white flowers before excusing herself, and we see a scarred Alicia– or Maelle– standing by as she watches the scene unfold, holding a sewn Esquie doll. The camera turns and we see the images of the very same Expeditioners, including Gustave and Verso’s painted self, framed by the Eiffel Tower as they wave goodbye before dissipating.

The colors are bright. It’s backlit by a sunny day. The comfort is uncertain and bittersweet, but it’s ultimately not an unwelcome feeling, either.

Undeniably, the discussion around these endings is, of course, typically viewed as black-and-white as possible. More often than not, when faced with multiple endings by the end of a game, audiences are used to getting a “good” ending and a “bad” ending, leaving little room for discussion. And, in these cases, that is the game’s intent. In these cases, the games do have a black-and-white, a good-and-bad. It’s not unheard of for a game to punish a player for making poor choices throughout a play through. When looking at Expedition 33’s endings, though, this mindset is frankly doing a disservice to the game’s theming as a whole.

Grief as a theme is interwoven throughout the entire game, and when is the process of grieving ever black-and-white? Grief by all accounts is an incredibly non-linear process. We have all grieved over someone, over something, and we all understand what that means. Both of the endings evoke very different emotions, but it really is up to the player and what they choose to prioritize within their own grief. Yes, in Maelle’s ending, we see the way she chooses to use her Paintress abilities against her brother and father’s wishes, but more importantly, she’s also surrounded by those she has come to love, in a fully-functioning body. She’s given grace to those who have only ever lived inside of the canvas, reasserting the idea that they are sentient individuals with their own lives and autonomy, despite the circumstances they were painted into. Within Verso’s ending, the Dessendre’s are now able to work on moving past their shared grief regarding the loss of their real-life brother and son after years of stagnation, but at the cost of Alicia having a healthy physical body, and at the loss of everyone we have come to love inside of the canvas.

Both of these endings offer a resolution and catharsis in their own ways, and the outcome of one doesn’t make the other more or less right. When discussing these endings, we can’t assume why someone chose one ending over the other, because their grief surrounding the game is ultimately their own, and it’s not up to us to dictate how that feels to them. It can’t be stressed enough how sacrificing nuance in these discussions doesn’t only do a disservice to the game, but also the players and their own emotions about it.

I have a confession to make: I wholeheartedly chose Maelle’s ending the first time I played, and at that moment, it wasn’t a difficult choice for me. It made sense. I had grown so incredibly fond of Lumiere and the canvas and those inside of it, just like Maelle, but I saw myself in so many facets of her. I was a sixteen-year-old girl once, finding escape in worlds I created and in the media I was in love with, be it novels or games or movies, in order to remove myself from the very real grief I was experiencing. It’s something I still find myself doing even in adulthood, and ironically, probably the reason why I found myself so absorbed in Expedition 33 in the first place. The hours I put into the game were the direct result of me needing a distraction from life, and to watch the game slowly begin to unveil what it truly was felt like looking into a mirror. Of course I chose to save Lumiere. Of course I sided with Maelle. It’s what I do all the time. More often than not, I run from my grief rather than let myself feel it, and instead I look for reassurance and acceptance and comfort in worlds where my real feelings can’t hurt me. It’s far easier to feel for the characters on my screen than it is to feel for myself. After all, their emotions aren’t tangible, unlike my own. Expedition 33 was the first time I had ever personally experienced a piece of media that conveyed that feeling in a way that felt so specific, and so undeniably real.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is now available in Arabic!
items.summary: Expeditioners! Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text! This brings the total number of supported langua
items.content:
Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: 1st Anniversary of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: Expeditioners!! Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special
items.content:
Expeditioners!! 

 

Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. 

 

To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special piece of artwork that we hope you will enjoy! 

8 Million Copies Sold

We're so thrilled, and honestly still quite overwhelmed, to announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has officially reached 8 million copies sold!

Thank you so so much to every single person who has played, created art, shared, streamed, discussed, and supported this game!!

Game Update: New Haircuts + Patch Notes

We've pushed a fun little update live today: new haircuts are now available in-game, giving the expedition even more style to strut around in! 💅 

For the full list of changes, fixes, and improvements, you can read the patch notes here

Community Emotes

Our community is packed with phenomenally talented artists and we wanted to celebrate that today.  

We commissioned some of our amazing community creators to design official Expedition 33 emotes for you to use in your own channels! 

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

Official Baguette Merch

In the mood to add some baguette to your wardrobe? 

We’ve partnered with Orcival and Le Béret Français to bring you the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 striped shirt and beret for your cosplays! 🥖    You can purchase the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Orcival mariniere here

And the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Le Béret Français beret is available to buy here

On top of that, keep an eye out for a limited number of units of the Monolith Set to be back in stock from our partners at Laced and Pix n' Love soon!! 

And Finally… Cake

It's been a big day for us. Thank you for making it possible. 🎂 

And if you know someone who wants to pick up the game, we're running a 20% sale right now on Steam - As well as some fun merchandise goodies available on our merch page!

Merch Page

From the bottom of our hearts, we’re so thankful to each and every one of you – this has been the best year of our lives, thanks to you. 

 

- The Expedition 33 Team
